analyses.question: Is Lake Volta the largest man-made lake — and by what measure?
analyses.approach: Compare published surface area and full-capacity storage for Lake Volta and Lake Kariba; draw both outlines on one Lambert azimuthal equal-area scale; simple arithmetic for the gap and the Polytank comparison.
analyses.finding: Volta is larger by surface area (8,502 vs 5,580 km2); Kariba stores more at full capacity (181 vs 148 km3, +33 km3). 148 trillion L / 5,000 L = 29.6 billion tanks.
analyses.repro_notes: Geometry prep: animations/remotion/scripts/prep_geo.py. Animation: animations/remotion (Remotion 4.0.543), see PROVENANCE.md.
analyses.limitations: Published mean depths (18.8 m, 29.2 m) do not reconcile exactly with area x capacity (17.4 m, 32.4 m implied), likely different water levels/survey dates; the video never shows area x depth = volume and labels depth visuals as illustration.

evidence.claim: Lake Volta is the largest man-made lake in the world by surface area, about 8,500 km2.
evidence.qualification: Published figure 8,502 km2, shown rounded. Qualified "by surface area" throughout.

evidence.claim: At full capacity Lake Volta holds about 148 km3 (148 trillion litres).
evidence.qualification: Full-capacity figure; actual storage varies with water level.

evidence.claim: Lake Kariba covers about 5,600 km2, a smaller area than Lake Volta.
At full capacity Lake Kariba holds about 181 km3 (181 trillion litres) — more than thirty cubic kilometres more than Lake Volta.
Lake Volta's water would fill almost 30 billion 5,000-litre tanks.
evidence.qualification: Arithmetic: 148e12 L / 5,000 L = 29.6e9. Generic tank drawing, no brand implied.

evidence.claim: Lake Kariba is on average about one and a half times as deep as Lake Volta.
evidence.qualification: Published mean depths 18.8 m vs 29.2 m. Depth gauges labelled as published means, not surveyed profiles; containers labelled illustration.
